goal.what: The developers build a product with which its users achieve their goals, each choice leaning on the few things that the vision names.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers know whom the product serves and what each of them is trying to achieve.

necessary_conditions.what: Does Roles list each kind of person who comes to the product to get its job done?
necessary_conditions.why: The developers build for the people Roles lists, so a missing role goes unserved, and two roles merged into one get a product that fits neither.

items.text: Find the job that the product exists to do in the steering's outcome and decisions, and, where the repository already holds the product, in what it already says the product does. Write it in one sentence as what the product gets done for the people who come to it, such as `turns a request into a deliverable that the people it's for can use`. Where none of these says it, ask the user what the product gets done, and for whom.
Name each kind of person who comes to the product for that job by the part of it they come to get done, such as `one who asks rn for a deliverable` in place of `developer`.
Ask whether that job gets done only if someone else also does a job with the product, such as an administrator who sets it up on a shared server for a team. Name each such person as a role as well.

For each person whose job the goal, the decisions, and what the product does leave unclear, ask the user `What does <person> come to the product to get done?`, with the job you'd guess as your recommendation.
Split a role where two of its members would count different results as their job done, such as a guest who browses a shop and a member who buys from it.
Merge two roles where their members would count the same result as their job done, such as a new customer and a returning customer who both buy from a shop.
Name the role `user` where there's only one.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each objective state, in one sentence, what one role is trying to achieve in their own work?
necessary_conditions.why: The developers build toward the objectives, so each must name the end that a role reaches in their own work, and neither a feature nor a measure of that end.

items.text: For each role, take its job from Roles and write it as the end the role reaches in their own work, in one sentence with the role as the subject, such as `the user gets each deliverable they mean`.

Ask why that end matters to the role, and ask again of each answer, until the answer is something the role reaches in their own work and no longer something the product does, such as going on from `rn writes the README` to `the people the README is for decide on the product with it`.
Write one objective for each distinct end, where two ends are distinct if a role can reach one without the other, such as a member who buys and an administrator who keeps the shop running.

Read each objective with the product's name taken out. Where it then reads as a feature, such as `manage tasks in the app`, rewrite it as the end the role reaches, such as `the team finishes its work on time`.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the vision describe only what the users do and get, not how the product works inside?
necessary_conditions.why: The vision must stay true while the inside of the product changes, so it describes only what the users do and get, and says nothing of how the product does it.

items.text: For each sentence of the vision, ask whether it would change if the product's insides changed while the users saw the same. If it would, take it out, and where it carried something the users see, write that in its place, such as `answers within a second` in place of `keeps an index in memory`.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers can tell whether a change brings the users closer to their goals.

necessary_conditions.what: Does each objective have a key result that measures how well its role achieves it, and one of how fast only where the time decides the objective, each with the direction that's better?
necessary_conditions.why: The developers keep a change only if it brings the users closer to their goals, so each objective needs measures that a developer reads after a change. Usability testers judge a change by the [success rate and the time on task](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/usability-metrics/) of each task the users do, and the key results take these, the time only where it decides whether the role reaches the objective, as a measure that decides nothing leans no change.

items.text: For each objective, write the task its role does to reach it, from where they start to the result they keep, such as from the user's request to the deliverable they sign off.

Make the first key result measure how well: the share of those tasks in which the role reaches the result. Where a run of the task shows the failures rather than the successes, such as a deliverable that its people can't use, measure the share that fails instead, such as `the share of the deliverables rn hands over that the people they're for couldn't use`.

Where the time decides whether the role reaches the objective, such as a task that's no use once late, make a second key result measure how fast: the time from the task's start to its result, the role's own time in it included, such as the time the user spends answering questions. Where that time depends mostly on things outside the product, such as the speed of the machine, count the role's own effort instead, such as the questions they answer.
Give each key result the direction that's better, such as `Lower is better.`, and no target, since developers who aim at a number improve the number in place of the users' result.
Rank the key results, how well before how fast, so that a developer keeps a change that improves one only if none ranked before it gets worse.

For each key result, write down what one end-to-end (E2E) run of the role's task would record that a developer counts the key result from, such as each deliverable that a judge marks unusable, or the times at which the task starts and ends. Where no record of such a run would show it, rewrite the key result.

necessary_conditions.what: Are the objectives distinct, so that each piece of work serves one of them?
necessary_conditions.why: The developers decide what to build by asking which objective a piece of work serves, which works only where each piece serves one objective.

items.text: Once each role has its objectives, and before you write any key result, list each piece of work the product plans that the steering's decisions name. Where the repository already holds the product, add each of its open issues and each feature it already gives its users.
For each piece of work, name each objective it serves, such as `O1` for `ask the user only what the best practice doesn't settle`.

For each pair of objectives, ask whether a piece of work could serve one without the other. If no piece could, merge the two into one objective, and name it in place of either wherever a piece names one of them.

For each piece that still names more than one objective, split it into parts that each serve one, such as `search and checkout` into `search` for the guest's objective and `checkout` for the member's. Where it doesn't split, name only the objective whose role would miss it most, such as the guest's for a faster first page, which a guest meets on every visit and a member once before checkout.

To keep only the work that serves an end, read, for each piece that serves no objective, what the request, the decisions, and the issue that asks for the piece say it's for. Where they name an end that no objective names, add the objective. Where they leave it open, ask the user `Is <piece> not needed, or does it serve an end that no objective names?`, with the answer you'd give as your recommendation.

critical_success_factors.what: The developers know the one way by which the product brings its users to their goals, so that every choice leans toward it.

necessary_conditions.what: Does the concept state first the one way by which the product brings the users to their objectives, and then only the ideas without which this way fails at a moment of their use?
necessary_conditions.why: The developers make many choices that no line of the vision names, and the concept lets each of them lean the same way, so that the users meet one product and not a set of parts that pull apart. The user gives the product's purpose and intent and decides by them, so the maker derives the concept from what they gave, and hands back only what it leaves open.

items.text: To find the one way that the user means, read what they gave of the product's purpose and intent: the steering's outcome and decisions, the user's words in the request and in their answers, and, where the repository already holds the product, what it already says of the product's purpose, and its open issues. List each way these say or imply that the product brings the roles to their objectives, such as a rule the user gave for when rn asks them, since the one way comes from whoever conceived the product, and an analysis of what goes wrong today yields only a list of fixes with no center.

To give the developers one way to lean on, write it in one sentence as what the users see the product do, such as `rn works only on the vital few, the things that decide whether the people a deliverable is for can use it`. Where the list holds several ways, take the one from which the others follow, and where none follows from another, the one that brings each role closest to its objective's first key result. Where the list holds none, take the way by which products that do the same job bring their users to such objectives, and fit it to the objectives.

To leave the user only the decision that's theirs, ask them about the one way only where what they gave and the field's practice leave two ways open that would lead the developers to different choices, or where the way is hard to undo or changes what other people share, such as a service that other teams use. Ask in terms of what the roles get, such as `Should <role> get <result> or <result> at <moment>?`, with the way you'd take as your recommendation and what it rests on.

To find where the one way must hold, list the moments of the users' use, from the moment they first meet the product to the moment they reach the objective, as a [customer journey map](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/journey-mapping-101/) does, such as the request, the goal confirmed, the questions answered, how each deliverable will be agreed, and each deliverable signed off.

To keep the one way holding at every moment, ask at each moment whether it holds there as it stands. Only where it fails, derive the idea that keeps it holding from the user's words, the repository's precedents, such as how the product already handles that moment, or the field's practice, and write the idea with what it gives the role toward the objective.

Ask the user about an idea only where those sources leave two ideas open that give the roles different results at that moment, or where the idea is hard to undo or changes what other people share, in the form that N6.3 asks in.

Keep only the ideas on which the one way stands, as the developers hold the concept in mind at every choice, and a list too long to hold leans no choice. Move an idea that carries out another, such as how a fix is made, out of the concept, to where the people who carry it out need it. Drop each idea where taking it out leaves the one way holding at every moment.

At each moment, take a design choice that no line of the vision names, such as whether to ask the user about a point the best practice settles, and decide it by the one way and its ideas. Where they don't decide it one way, rewrite the idea for that moment until they do.
